## Introduction

For this project, I analyzed the expression of three genes, *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3*, across 157 pregnancy samples. I used maternal BMI as my continuous variable and pregnancy status as my first categorical variable. I created a second categorical variable by dividing maternal BMI into two groups, below 25 and 25 or higher. I created an R function to generate a histogram, scatterplot, and grouped boxplot for each gene, giving a total of nine plots. I then compared the gene expression patterns across the three genes.


```{r, include=FALSE}
# I loaded the three original datasets.
# The first column of the expression file contains probe IDs.
covar <- read.csv("GSE85307_covar-1.csv")

gene_expression <- read.csv(
  "GSE85307_geneExpression.csv",
  row.names = 1,
  check.names = FALSE
)
gene_names <- read.csv("GSE85307_geneNames.csv")
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# I changed maternal BMI from text to numbers.
covar$BMI <- as.numeric(
  sub(".*: ", "", as.character(covar$mat_BMI))
)

# I kept pregnancy status as a categorical variable.
covar$Pregnancy_Status <- factor(
  sub(".*: ", "", covar$preg_preeclampsia)
)

# I divided BMI into two groups using 25 as the cutoff.
covar$BMI_Category <- factor(
  ifelse(covar$BMI < 25, "BMI < 25", "BMI >= 25")
)

```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# I used the same three genes from Submission 2.
selected_genes <- c("CNR1", "SOCS5", "SIRT3")

# I matched gene names to probe IDs using the lookup file.
gene_lookup <- gene_names[
  gene_names$GENE %in% selected_genes,
  c("PROBEID", "GENE")
]

# I checked whether each probe ID is in the expression data.
gene_lookup$Available <- as.character(gene_lookup$PROBEID) %in%
  rownames(gene_expression)

# I checked that all three genes have expression data.
stopifnot(all(selected_genes %in% gene_lookup$GENE[gene_lookup$Available]))

# I checked that the sample IDs match across both datasets.
stopifnot(all(covar$geoID %in% colnames(gene_expression)))
```

```{r, include=FALSE}

# Created a reusable function to plot multiple genes.
# The function accepts a data frame, gene names,
# one continuous variable and two categorical variables.

create_gene_plots <- function(data, genes,
                              continuous_var,
                              categorical_vars) {

  # Store the resulting plots in a list.
  all_plots <- list()

  # Repeat the analysis for every selected gene.
  for (gene in genes) {

    # Find the probe ID automatically.
    probe_id <- as.character(
      gene_names$PROBEID[gene_names$GENE == gene]
    )

    # Check that the gene has an available probe.
    probe_id <- probe_id[
      probe_id %in% rownames(gene_expression)
    ]

    if (length(probe_id) == 0) {
      stop(paste("No expression data for", gene))
    }

    # Match expression values to sample IDs.
    plot_data <- data

    plot_data$Expression <- as.numeric(
      gene_expression[probe_id[1], plot_data$geoID]
    )

    # Create the histogram.
    histogram <- ggplot(
      plot_data, aes(x = Expression)
    ) +
      geom_histogram(
        bins = 20,
        fill = "#4472A0",
        color = "white"
      ) +
      labs(
        title = bquote("Distribution of" ~ italic(.(gene)) ~ "expression"),
        x = bquote(italic(.(gene)) ~ "gene expression"),
        y = "Number of Samples"
      ) +
      theme_classic(base_size = 13)

    # Create the scatterplot.
    scatterplot <- ggplot(
      plot_data,
      aes(x = .data[[continuous_var]], y = Expression)
    ) +
      geom_point(color = "#4472A0", alpha = 0.7) +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
                  color = "#C0504D") +
      labs(
        title = bquote("Maternal BMI vs." ~ italic(.(gene))),
        x = "Maternal BMI (kg/m²)",
        y = bquote(italic(.(gene)) ~ "gene expression")
      ) +
      theme_classic(base_size = 13)

    # Create the grouped boxplot.
    boxplot <- ggplot(
      plot_data,
      aes(
        x = .data[[categorical_vars[1]]],
        y = Expression,
        fill = .data[[categorical_vars[2]]]
      )
    ) +
      geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(0.8)) +
      scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("#4472A0", "#E69F00")
      ) +
      labs(
        title = bquote(italic(.(gene)) ~ "expression by pregnancy status and BMI"),
        x = "Pregnancy Status",
        y = bquote(italic(.(gene)) ~ "gene expression"),
        fill = "BMI Category"
      ) +
      theme_classic(base_size = 13)

    # Save all three plots for this gene.
    all_plots[[gene]] <- list(
      histogram = histogram,
      scatterplot = scatterplot,
      boxplot = boxplot
    )
  }

  return(all_plots)
}
```

```{r make-plots, include=FALSE}
# I ran the same plotting function for all three genes.
library(ggplot2)
all_gene_plots <- create_gene_plots(
  data = covar,
  genes = selected_genes,
  continuous_var = "BMI",
  categorical_vars = c("Pregnancy_Status", "BMI_Category")
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Compare gene expression across the three selected genes.
# Automatically find each gene's probe ID and match samples by geoID.

gene_summary <- data.frame()

for (gene in selected_genes) {

  # Find the probe ID for this gene.
  probe_id <- as.character(
    gene_names$PROBEID[gene_names$GENE == gene]
  )

  # Keep only probes available in the expression dataset.
  probe_id <- probe_id[
    probe_id %in% rownames(gene_expression)
  ]

  # Extract expression values in the correct sample order.
  expression_values <- as.numeric(
    gene_expression[probe_id[1], covar$geoID]
  )

  # Calculate descriptive statistics.
  gene_summary <- rbind(
    gene_summary,
    data.frame(
      Gene = gene,
      Mean = mean(expression_values, na.rm = TRUE),
      Median = median(expression_values, na.rm = TRUE),
      SD = sd(expression_values, na.rm = TRUE),
      Minimum = min(expression_values, na.rm = TRUE),
      Maximum = max(expression_values, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
}

# I rounded the results and put them in a table.
gene_summary[, -1] <- round(gene_summary[, -1], 3)
knitr::kable(gene_summary, caption = "Descriptive statistics for three genes", booktabs = TRUE)
```

## Comparison of Gene Expression Across Three Genes

I compared *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3* using their mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum expression values across 157 pregnancy samples.

*SIRT3* had the highest average expression value (8.916), followed by *SOCS5* (7.474) and *CNR1* (4.873).

*SOCS5* had the highest standard deviation (0.146), suggesting slightly more variation in its expression values. *SIRT3* had the lowest standard deviation (0.123), suggesting slightly less variation.

*CNR1* had the largest difference between its minimum and maximum expression values, mainly because a few samples had higher expression values.

Overall, the three genes showed different expression distributions. These results describe expression patterns within the dataset and do not establish biological or statistical significance.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Compare the relationship between maternal BMI
# and gene expression for all three selected genes.

correlation_results <- data.frame()

for (gene in selected_genes) {

  # Automatically find the gene's probe ID.
  probe_id <- as.character(
    gene_names$PROBEID[gene_names$GENE == gene]
  )

  # Select a probe available in the expression dataset.
  probe_id <- probe_id[
    probe_id %in% rownames(gene_expression)
  ][1]

  # Match expression values to the correct samples.
  expression_values <- as.numeric(
    gene_expression[probe_id, covar$geoID]
  )

  # Calculate Pearson correlation with maternal BMI.
  correlation <- cor(
    covar$BMI,
    expression_values,
    use = "complete.obs",
    method = "pearson"
  )

  # Store the result for each gene.
  correlation_results <- rbind(
    correlation_results,
    data.frame(
      Gene = gene,
      BMI_Correlation = round(correlation, 3)
    )
  )
}

# I put the correlations in a table.
knitr::kable(correlation_results, caption = "Pearson correlations with maternal BMI", booktabs = TRUE)
```

## Comparison of Maternal BMI and Gene Expression

I calculated Pearson correlations to compare the relationship between maternal BMI and the expression of *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3* across 157 pregnancy samples.

*CNR1* had a correlation of -0.093, showing a very weak negative relationship with maternal BMI. *SOCS5* had a correlation of 0.084, showing a very weak positive relationship. *SIRT3* had a correlation of -0.039, which was closest to zero.

Overall, all three correlations were very weak. This suggests that maternal BMI had little linear association with the expression of these genes in this dataset. These results do not establish causation or statistical significance.

## Comparison of Gene Expression by Pregnancy Status and BMI

I compared *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3* expression across normal pregnancies and pregnancies with preeclampsia. I also compared two BMI categories: below 25 and 25 or higher.

For *CNR1*, the median expression values were similar across all four groups. The BMI below 25 groups showed slightly higher median expression.

For *SOCS5*, participants with BMI 25 or higher generally had higher median expression values, especially among those with preeclampsia.

For *SIRT3*, the median expression values were also similar across the four groups, although the BMI 25 or higher groups showed slightly higher median values.

Overall, all three genes showed overlapping expression distributions across pregnancy status and BMI categories. The observed differences were relatively small, and these plots alone do not establish statistical significance.

## Comparison of Histograms Across Three Genes

I compared the distributions of *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3* gene expression across 157 pregnancy samples.

*CNR1* had most expression values around 4.8 to 4.9. Its distribution was slightly right-skewed, with a few samples showing higher expression values.

*SOCS5* had most expression values around 7.4 to 7.6. Its distribution was more balanced around the center and showed slightly greater variation.

*SIRT3* had most expression values around 8.8 to 9.0. Its distribution was more concentrated around the center, with a few values at either end.

Overall, the three genes showed different expression distributions. *SOCS5* had the largest standard deviation (0.146), while *SIRT3* had the smallest (0.123).

## Summary statistics by pregnancy status

```{r maternal-summary, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# I used gtsummary to compare the two pregnancy groups.

library(dplyr)
library(gtsummary)

# Prepare variables for the table
table_data <- covar %>%
  mutate(
    mat_age_yrs = as.numeric(
      sub(".*: ", "", mat_age_yrs)
    ),
    mat_BMI = as.numeric(
      sub(".*: ", "", mat_BMI)
    ),
    delivery_gestAge_wks = as.numeric(
      sub(".*: ", "", delivery_gestAge_wks)
    ),
    Pregnancy_Status = factor(Pregnancy_Status),
    BMI_Category = factor(BMI_Category)
  )

# Create summary statistics table
summary_table <- table_data %>%
  select(
    Pregnancy_Status,
    mat_age_yrs,
    mat_BMI,
    delivery_gestAge_wks,
    BMI_Category
  ) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = Pregnancy_Status,
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
    ),
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 2,
    label = list(
      mat_age_yrs ~ "Maternal Age (years)",
      mat_BMI ~ "Maternal BMI",
      delivery_gestAge_wks ~ "Gestational Age at Delivery (weeks)",
      BMI_Category ~ "BMI Category"
    )
  ) %>%
  add_overall()

# I added a caption to the table.
summary_table <- summary_table %>%
  modify_caption("**Maternal characteristics by pregnancy status**")
summary_table
```

The dataset included 157 pregnancy samples, with 110 normal pregnancies and 47 cases of preeclampsia. The preeclampsia group had a higher average maternal BMI (31.16 versus 27.99) and a lower average gestational age at delivery (37.81 versus 39.25 weeks). These are descriptive differences.

## Heatmap of ten genes

```{r ten-gene-heatmap, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Heatmap of standardized expression for ten genes across 157 samples, with hierarchical clustering and pregnancy status and BMI category annotations."}
# I used pheatmap to compare expression patterns across ten genes.
library(pheatmap)


# Match available gene names with expression probe IDs
available_genes <- gene_names[
  as.character(gene_names$PROBEID) %in%
    rownames(gene_expression),
  c("PROBEID", "GENE")
]

# Keep genes with valid names
available_genes <- available_genes[
  !is.na(available_genes$GENE) &
    available_genes$GENE != "",
]

# Select 10 genes
heatmap_genes <- available_genes[1:10, ]

# Match probe IDs to expression rows
probe_ids <- as.character(heatmap_genes$PROBEID)

heatmap_data <- gene_expression[
  match(probe_ids, rownames(gene_expression)),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Use gene names as row labels
rownames(heatmap_data) <- heatmap_genes$GENE

# Match samples by geoID
sample_order <- match(
  colnames(heatmap_data),
  covar$geoID
)

stopifnot(!anyNA(sample_order))

# Create two categorical annotations
annotation_data <- data.frame(
  Pregnancy = factor(
    covar$Pregnancy_Status[sample_order]
  ),
  BMI = factor(
    covar$BMI_Category[sample_order]
  )
)

rownames(annotation_data) <- colnames(heatmap_data)

# Convert expression values to numeric
heatmap_matrix <- as.matrix(heatmap_data)
storage.mode(heatmap_matrix) <- "numeric"

# Check for missing values
stopifnot(!anyNA(heatmap_matrix))

# Generate heatmap
pheatmap(
  heatmap_matrix,
  scale = "row",
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  cluster_cols = TRUE,
  annotation_col = annotation_data,
  show_colnames = FALSE,
  labels_row = parse(text = paste0("italic('", rownames(heatmap_matrix), "')")),
  main = "Gene Expression Across Pregnancy Samples",
  fontsize_row = 10
)
```

The heatmap shows how expression varies across the samples. I scaled each gene by row and used clustering to group similar patterns. The colored bars identify pregnancy status and BMI category. I did not see a clear separation between pregnancy groups based on this plot alone.

## Additional visualization: Parallel coordinates plot

```{r parallel-plot, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Parallel coordinates plot of standardized expression for three genes. Thin lines show individual samples and thick lines show the mean profile within each pregnancy group."}
# I used the same three genes to compare individual expression profiles.
parallel_data <- data.frame()
for (gene in selected_genes) {
  # I matched the probe ID and kept the sample order the same.
  probe_id <- as.character(gene_lookup$PROBEID[
    gene_lookup$GENE == gene & gene_lookup$Available
  ][1])
  gene_data <- data.frame(
    geoID = covar$geoID,
    Gene = gene,
    Expression = as.numeric(gene_expression[probe_id, covar$geoID]),
    Pregnancy_Status = covar$Pregnancy_Status
  )
  parallel_data <- rbind(parallel_data, gene_data)
}

# I standardized each gene so their expression patterns are comparable.
parallel_data$Scaled_Expression <- ave(
  parallel_data$Expression,
  parallel_data$Gene,
  FUN = function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))
)
parallel_data$Gene <- factor(parallel_data$Gene, levels = selected_genes)

# I drew a thin line for each sample and a thicker mean line for each group.
ggplot(parallel_data,
       aes(x = Gene, y = Scaled_Expression,
           group = geoID, color = Pregnancy_Status)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = Pregnancy_Status),
               fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ Pregnancy_Status) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) {
    parse(text = paste0("italic('", x, "')"))
  }) +
  labs(
    title = "Gene Expression Profiles Across Pregnancy Samples",
    subtitle = "Standardized expression for three genes",
    x = "Gene", y = "Standardized gene expression",
    color = "Pregnancy status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

I used a parallel coordinates plot to compare *CNR1*, *SOCS5*, and *SIRT3* across the two pregnancy groups. Each thin line shows a sample, and the thicker line shows the group average. The average profiles were fairly similar across groups. This plot alone does not show statistical significance.
